title: The second paragraph (Deuteronomy 11:13–21)
hookLine: what we do affects the rain and the harvest

cards: The Shema doesn't stop at its first line, or at the paragraph after it: love the LORD your God with all your heart, teach these words to your children, write them on your doorposts. It has three paragraphs.
The second comes from later in Deuteronomy, and it sounds like a farmer's almanac with a warning label. Rain in its season. Grass for the cattle.
Then a hard turn: what the people do reaches the sky and the soil.

teach.b: It opens, in the old Jewish translation: "And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto My commandments which I command you this day, to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul."
If you do, then rain: "the former rain and the latter rain," grain and wine and oil, grass for your animals.
If your heart turns away to other gods, the sky closes, the land gives no harvest, and you are lost from the good land.
Then it repeats the commands from the first paragraph: these words on your heart, on your hand, on your doorposts, taught to your children. Three things stand out. First, the grammar.
The first paragraph speaks to you, singular.
This one speaks mostly to you, plural: a whole community, together. Second, the order.

The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, explains why this paragraph comes second: first a person accepts the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. Third, the phrase serve him with all your heart.

teach.h: SERVICE OF THE HEART IS PRAYER.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, asks: what is service of the heart? And answers: prayer. The phrase you met a few weeks ago, avodah shebalev, comes from here.
The idea that rain answers obedience has troubled readers, and Jewish movements have handled it differently. The classic Reform prayer book left this paragraph out.
Orthodox and Conservative prayer books keep it, and newer Reform prayer books often offer it again.
Some readers today hear it simply: what we do, together, reaches the land.

how: The second paragraph of the Shema, Deuteronomy 11:13–21, is said morning and evening after the first; in some Reform prayer books it is optional or replaced, while Orthodox and Conservative prayer books include it.

games.why: Rabbi Joshua ben Korcha: a person first accepts the kingdom of heaven, then the commandments.

practice: Think of one small thing you did yesterday, a meal you cooked, something you threw away, a word said in anger or in kindness, and follow it outward. Whose rain grew the food, where did the trash go, who carried that word home?
Follow it two or three steps, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart — the Talmud's name for prayer, drawn from the Shema's second paragraph: serve Him with all your heart.

orig.note: Hebrew: and it shall be, if you hearken, the opening words of the second paragraph.
